title: Viswanathan Anand Becomes First Indian to Lead World Chess Body as Interim FIDE President
excerpt: The five-time world champion steps into the top role after Arkady Dvorkovich suspends duties following EU sanctions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
body:
• Viswanathan Anand becomes the first Indian to serve as FIDE President, taking over on an interim basis after Arkady Dvorkovich's suspension.
  • Dvorkovich voluntarily stepped aside after being placed on the EU's 21st sanctions package linked to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
  • FIDE's presidential election is scheduled for September at the Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
  • Anand has served as FIDE Deputy President since August 2022 and is a five-time World Chess Champion.

Viswanathan Anand, the five-time World Chess Champion from Chennai, has been elevated to the role of interim president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE), becoming the first Indian ever to hold the position. The move follows the voluntary suspension of Russian incumbent Arkady Dvorkovich, who stepped aside on Friday after being placed on the European Union's latest sanctions list.

Dvorkovich Steps Down Under EU Pressure

The EU's 21st sanctions package, issued in connection with Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, imposes punitive measures against 170 entities and 48 individuals, according to Reuters. Measures include potential asset freezes, travel bans, and transaction restrictions.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DbAI7mxDT8u/

Dvorkovich, a former Russian deputy prime minister who has led FIDE since 2018, denounced the EU move as "unlawful and unfair" in a statement posted on the FIDE website. He pledged to challenge the sanctions through all available legal means.

"Given that until a formal court decision is rendered and/or such decision is cancelled or amended, these sanctions could hinder the stable functioning of FIDE, I have decided to voluntarily suspend the exercise of my powers and duties as FIDE President with immediate effect."

— Arkady Dvorkovich, FIDE President

Despite stepping aside, Dvorkovich had indicated last month that he would seek re-election to the presidency. The election is scheduled to take place at FIDE's general assembly during September's Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Multiple candidates have already announced their bids, including Russian-Kazakh businessman Timur Turlov and former FIDE president Kirsan Ilyumzhinov.

Anand's Rise from Deputy to Interim President

Anand was elected as FIDE Deputy President in August 2022 during the FIDE Congress held alongside the 44th Chess Olympiad in Chennai. He was part of Dvorkovich's electoral team and received strong backing from the chess community. The FIDE Council elevated him to the presidency on an interim basis following Dvorkovich's suspension announcement on July 23.

https://x.com/FIDE_chess/status/2080404859359310185

The 56-year-old grandmaster holds an extraordinary record in competitive chess. He became India's first grandmaster in 1988, won the FIDE World Chess Championship in 2000, and held the undisputed world title from 2007 to 2013. He has also been a two-time World Rapid Chess Champion and won the World Blitz Chess Cup. In 1991, he became the first recipient of the Khel Ratna Award, India's highest sporting honour, and was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 2007.

Broader Sanctions Context

The EU's sanctions package also placed Mikhail Degtyarev, Russian Sports Minister and head of the country's national Olympic committee, on the list. FIDE had already suspended Russia on June 11 following a Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling.

The sanctions underscore a widening rift between Russian-led sports bodies and Western institutions. For FIDE, the timing adds complexity to an already crowded presidential race, with the Samarkand election set to determine the federation's long-term direction.

What It Means for Indian Chess

Anand's appointment, even in an interim capacity, marks a symbolic milestone for Indian chess, a sport he almost single-handedly popularised in the country. With Indian players now dominating at every level — from D. Gukesh's challenge for the classical world title to R. Praggnanandhaa's rapid rise — having an Indian at the helm of world chess's governing body reflects the country's growing influence in the sport. For the global Indian diaspora, which has watched Anand compete on the world stage for over three decades, the moment carries particular resonance.
